title: Oberlin epiphany and the 2006 symphony commission
summary: Reading Blues People sparked the idea of a Chinese-American symphony; forty years later Michael Morgan helped get it commissioned and premiered in 2007 and 2008.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Yeah. So how did I get to that. So anyway, I read a passage in Blues People by Leroi Jones, who is now known as Amiri Baraka. And in those days, I’m talking about the mid- 70’s, 1975, 1977, there were only two books on the reading list. There were probably a few more. But there was Blues People by Leroi Jones, and then The Music of Black Americans by Eileen Southern. So there weren’t that many. And I remember in the book by Amiri Baraka he talked about Africans brought over here as slaves, and they brought their songs with them. And then he mentioned that, but the feeling of doing labor in your own country is different than forced labor in another country. So that got me to thinking about well what about the Chinese who were brought over to the United States. Did they sing work songs and what did they sound like? So after the class was over I left the conservatory and I saw this sculpture of the underground railroad. Oberlin was a destination point for the underground railroad. And so there was a sculpture built. And I had this epiphany about someday composing a Chinese-American symphony. So 40 years later this dream came about when I was at an arts conference in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And I bumped into an Oberlin classmate who was a conductor, Michael Morgan. And we didn’t have a personal relationship. We had I think, we were really no different. He was a conductor in European music, I was studying piano performance. But I was interested in many different kinds of music. I was in a Javanese gamelan ensemble, a West African kora music ensemble, I studied composition, I performed in jazz ensembles, but I was a piano performance major, primarily eighteenth and nineteenth western European classical music. And I started late, at the age of 19. So I only had like two years under my belt. And that was considered taboo, to be exploring music outside of the eighteenth- nineteenth century western European hegemon. So it was a struggle and very, kind of stressful. But I saw it was very weary, the battle. I would describe it as an arts apartheid, or arts aparteid. I mean Stevie Wonder and those who were involved in South African liberation and struggles like in the 1980’s, we would pronounce it apartheid, not aparteid. But I mean I was active in that. That was one of the many struggles I was involved in as a political activist. But anyway, going back to my experience at Oberlin, as I said, yeah, 40 years later Michael Morgan, who was a conductor, he — somehow I introduced this idea to him and he thought well this would fit perfectly with the Sacramento Philharmonic Orchestra, which recently just received some funding for this California initiative to celebrate the history of California. And so the Sacramento Philharmonic Orchestra and the Oakland East Bay Symphony commissioned me to compose this work in 2006, and the work premiered, ironically, on the day that the Chinese set the record for laying down tracks in a single day, the number of miles, ten miles of track in a day. It beat the Irish, who were doing the Union Pacific Railroad. And that was April 28, 2007.
